title: All one (Galatians 3:26–28)
hookLine: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female

cards: In the story Acts tells, the first followers of Jesus were Jews. Then Gentiles began to believe too, and a hard question split the young movement.
Did a Gentile have to become Jewish first, be circumcised and take on the law of Moses, to belong fully? In the churches of Galatia, in what's now central Turkey, teachers were saying yes.
Paul, a Jew himself and proud of it, was saying no. The letter to the Galatians is the heat of that argument. And in the middle of it, Paul writes a sentence that still startles.

teach.b: He starts with what makes someone belong: "For you are all the children of God by faith, in Christ Jesus."

teach.h: BAPTIZED: YOU HAVE PUT ON CHRIST.
teach.b: Then baptism: "For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ." Put on, like clothing.
And then: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus."
Those three pairs were lines that divided the world Paul lived in: people, status, sex. Notice the third pair is worded differently from the first two.
In the Greek it reads, literally, no male and female: the words of Genesis, where God creates them male and female. Paul is reaching back to creation. And notice what he doesn't say.
He doesn't say the differences vanish. In his letters he still writes to slaves and masters, husbands and wives, Jews and Greeks, as who they are.
What he says is that in Christ none of these decides who belongs, or who ranks higher.

teach.h: ONE: NOT A BLEND, ONE PERSON.
teach.b: The word one, in Greek, is masculine: not one thing, a blend, but one person, as if all of them together were one new man in Christ. Catholics see this at the font.

teach.h: YOU ARE ALL ONE IN CHRIST JESUS.
teach.b: In the rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment, a sign that they have put on Christ. A child, an elderly convert, a prince, a refugee: the same water, the same white cloth.
Christians have taken centuries, and are still taking them, to live out what this sentence says.

how: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment as a sign of having put on Christ; the same rite is used for every person, whatever their rank.

games.q: teachers in Galatia say Gentile believers must first become Jewish to belong fully. you're Paul. what do you write?
o: say faith and baptism make them children of God, all one in Christ.
tell the Gentiles to start their own movement.
games.why: "there is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus."

practice: Picture the people you'll see today: at home, at work, on the bus, the person who serves your coffee.
Notice, without scolding yourself, who you put higher and who you barely see, then picture them all in the same white garment, at the same font.
If you pray, pray for the ones you usually overlook; if not, hold them all in the same light for a moment.

wordCard.voice: All one. Paul's sentence to the Galatians: neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, but all one in Christ Jesus. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: one, in the masculine form. Galatians 3:28: not 'one thing' but 'one' person in Christ.
